idiom_name: std::views::filter | transform | take | drop | iota pipeline
implementation_notes: Modern C++ replaced the hand-written lazy list with range adaptors: std::views::filter/transform/take/drop compose with operator| and evaluate per element, and std::views::iota generates a bounded or unbounded sequence, so the classic structure is a view pipeline that describes work without performing it. Views are non-owning and not memoized - the adaptor keeps the source by reference and recomputes on every traversal - so they are right for one-pass consumption of large or generated ranges, while a caching iterator remains justified when elements must be shared between consumers.
pitfalls: Views do not own their source: constructing a view over a temporary or a container that dies before iteration dangles (a classic dangling std::string_view/ranges bug).
Adaptor chains are not memoized - iterating a view twice recomputes every element, and a view of a mutated container observes the mutation.
Beware capturing lambda lifetime: a predicate or transform capturing by reference must outlive the view object that stores it.

variants.name: std::generator stackless coroutine (C++23)
variants.implementation_notes: C++23's std::generator turns a coroutine into a lazy sequence: the function body suspends at co_yield and resumes on each increment, so the producing code reads sequentially while the consumer pulls one element at a time, and the range can be composed with C++20 views. The generator is move-only and single-use, and the coroutine frame lives until the generator is destroyed, so it is the right realization for complex per-element logic over unbounded sources; prefer views when the transformation is a simple adaptor chain and no suspension is needed.
pitfalls: std::generator is a single-pass input range: copying/multi-pass algorithms and ranges::sort/unique on an infinite generator never terminate or fail concepts.
The coroutine frame is only released when the generator is destroyed - detaching or leaking the generator retains everything it captured.
C++23 coroutine support is uneven across compilers and standard libraries; ship the view-based variant when the toolchain floor is C++20.

variants.name: Hand-written memoizing lazy list (C++11)
variants.idiom_name: node with mutable std::optional<T>/std::function thunk + shared tail
variants.implementation_notes: When elements must be computed once and shared (expensive derivations, repeated traversal, persisted caches), a hand-written lazy list still beats views: a node holds a thunk plus a cached value, computes it exactly once and shares the immutable tail, giving memoized call-by-need semantics like Scala's LazyList. The cost is real ownership plumbing (shared_ptr/optional), thread-safety work if multiple threads force the same node, and retention: holding the head retains every realized element.
pitfalls: Holding the head while traversing a huge memoizing list retains the whole realized prefix (the classic lazy-list space leak).
A shared_ptr-based tail plus a thunk capturing the previous node creates reference cycles or unbounded retention if the producer closes over `this`.
Forcing the same node from two threads without a once-guard computes twice or races; use std::call_once/once_flag per node or document single-threaded forcing.
